desc:
You must choose at least one element of nums, and you may never choose two elements that sit next to each other (indices i and i + 1 cannot both be chosen). Return the largest possible sum of the chosen elements.

Values can be negative. For example, in [2, -1, 5, -4, 3] the best choice is 2 + 5 + 3 = 10, while in [-3, -1, -2] the best you can do is pick the single element -1.
constraints: At least one element must be chosen
hints: Look at the last element. Either it is part of the selection or it is not. What does each case leave you with?
Let best(i) be the best sum using only the first i elements. Then best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i-1]). Starting from an empty selection (sum 0) lets the DP skip negative numbers for free.

That DP may end with an empty selection, which is not allowed. If the array has at least one positive element, the empty selection can never be the best one. If every element is 0 or negative, the answer is simply the maximum element.
editorial: This is House Robber with two twists: values can be negative, and the selection must not be empty. First handle the twist that makes the answer trivial: if max(nums) ≤ 0, adding any second element can only make the sum smaller or equal, so the best choice is the single largest element.

Otherwise some element is positive, so a non-empty selection with a positive sum exists and the classic recurrence take = skip + x, skip = max(take, skip) (which allows the empty selection) returns a positive value that is automatically non-empty. Time O(n), space O(1).
